name: AI for Creators and Influencers
objectives: Using an AI assistant for ideas, write a niche statement, three content pillars and a 7-day content plan, so each post in the plan fits one of the pillars
Given samples of your own captions or speech, write a short video script with a strong hook with AI help, so it sounds like you when read out loud and every fact is checked

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Your niche and content pillars
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a niche statement and three content pillars for your channel.
This lesson builds toward: Using an AI assistant for ideas, you will write a niche statement, three content pillars and a 7-day content plan, so each post in the plan fits one of the pillars.
Audiences follow creators who are clearly about something. A niche statement says who you make content for and what they get: "Budget home cooking for college students", "Beginner weightlifting for women over 40", "Small-business tips for barbers".
Content pillars are the three or four topics you return to again and again. For budget cooking: cheap recipes, grocery hacks, kitchen basics, and day-in-my-life. Pillars make planning easy and help the audience know what to expect.
Ask AI: "My niche is [niche]. Suggest five content pillars and ten video ideas for each." Keep the ideas that match your real experience and personality; your voice is what AI cannot copy.
Step by step:
- Write who you make content for and what they get.
- Ask AI for five possible pillars and ideas for each.
- Choose three pillars that fit your real experience.
- Make a 7-day plan from the ideas.
Words to know:
- Niche: the specific topic and audience your content serves.
- Content pillar: a main topic you post about again and again.
Try it now: Write your niche statement, choose three pillars with AI's help, and build a 7-day content plan.
You can now define your niche and plan content around clear pillars.

check.q: What does a niche statement tell people?
options: How many followers you have
Which apps you use
Who you make content for and what they get
How often you post
check.why: A niche statement names your audience and what they get from you.

check.q: AI suggests a post idea that does not fit any of your three pillars. What would you do?
options: Post it anyway because AI suggested it
Skip it or reshape it to fit a pillar
Add a new pillar for every idea
Delete your pillars and start again
check.why: Pillars keep your plan focused, so ideas should fit one of them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Scripting with AI in your own voice
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a short video script with a strong hook, with AI help, that sounds like you.
This lesson builds toward: Given samples of your own captions or speech, you will write a short video script with a strong hook with AI help, so it sounds like you when read out loud and every fact is checked.
Short videos live or die in the first seconds. The hook is the opening line that makes people stay: a surprising fact, a bold promise you can keep, or a question your audience is already asking.
Help AI sound like you: paste two of your own captions or a transcript of you talking, and say "Match this voice." Then ask: "Write a 45-second script on [idea]. Give me five hook options, then the script with a clear point and a call to action." Pick a hook and edit the script out loud.
Check facts, especially on health, money, fitness or legal topics. AI can make up studies and numbers. If you cannot confirm a fact, cut it or say where viewers can check it.
Step by step:
- Give AI samples of your real voice.
- Ask for five hooks and a short script.
- Choose a hook and read the script out loud.
- Edit until it sounds like you.
- Check every fact; cut what you cannot confirm.
Words to know:
- Hook: the opening line that makes people keep watching.
- Call to action: what you ask viewers to do next, like follow or comment.
- Transcript: the written words of something spoken.
Try it now: Write one 45-second script with AI help using samples of your own voice. Choose a hook, read it out loud, edit it, and check every fact.
You can now script content with AI that grabs attention and sounds like you.

check.q: What is the job of a script's hook?
options: To keep people watching from the first line
To list your sponsors
To end the video
To show your channel name
check.why: The hook is the opening line that makes people stay.

check.q: AI's script sounds stiff and nothing like you. What would you do?
options: Post it as it is
Ask AI to make it longer
Give AI samples of your own words, then read it aloud and edit
Use a different topic
check.why: Your own samples and a read-aloud edit make the script sound like you.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Editing and repurposing with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn one long video or post into several short pieces with captions.
This lesson builds toward: Given one long video or post, you will repurpose it into at least three short pieces with captions, with every caption error fixed and each piece making sense alone.
Repurposing means turning one piece of content into many. A 10-minute video can become three short clips, a carousel post, a newsletter paragraph and a few quotes. AI tools can find highlight moments, cut clips, add captions and resize for each platform.
Many editing apps (for example CapCut, Canva, Descript or your platform's own editor) now include AI features such as auto-captions, background removal and clip suggestions. Features and plans change; check each app's help pages.
Always review AI captions for errors, especially names, numbers and slang, and check that a clip still makes sense on its own and does not twist what you or a guest said.
Step by step:
- Choose one long video or post.
- Use AI to find three to five highlight moments.
- Cut clips and add auto-captions.
- Fix caption errors and resize for each platform.
- Write a caption for each with AI help.
Words to know:
- Repurpose: turn one piece of content into several others.
- Auto-captions: subtitles made automatically from the audio.
- Carousel: a post with several images people swipe through.
Try it now: Repurpose one long video or post into at least three short pieces with captions. Fix every caption error.
You can now repurpose content with AI tools while keeping it accurate.

options: Deleting old posts
Copying another creator's video
Posting the same clip on one day many times
Turning one piece of content into several pieces
check.why: Repurposing makes several pieces, like short clips, from one long piece.

check.q: You cut a short clip, but alone it makes the guest seem to say the opposite of what they meant. What would you do?
options: Post it because it will get views
Choose a different cut that keeps their real meaning
Add a caption saying it was edited
Post it only on one platform
check.why: A short clip must make sense alone and not twist what was said.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Labeling AI content on platforms
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Decide when a platform requires you to label realistic AI content, and label it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of posts and your platform's rules, you will decide which posts need an AI label and write a labeling checklist, labeling every realistic AI post and labeling when unsure.
Platforms are adding rules for AI content. YouTube, for example, requires creators to disclose content that seems realistic and was made or meaningfully altered with AI: making a real person appear to say or do something they did not, altering footage of a real event or place, or generating a realistic scene that did not happen. You disclose with the AI-use setting when uploading.
YouTube does not require disclosure for clearly unrealistic content, minor edits like color fixes, beauty filters or background blur, or using AI for ideas, scripts, titles or thumbnails. Creators who repeatedly fail to disclose can face labels, removal or loss of partner program access.
Other platforms, such as TikTok and Meta's apps, have their own labeling rules; check each platform's help pages. When unsure, label it: honesty keeps your audience's trust.
Step by step:
- Ask: does this look realistic, and did AI make or meaningfully change it?
- If yes, use the platform's AI label or disclosure setting.
- Check each platform's help page for its rules.
- When unsure, label it.
Words to know:
- Synthetic content: images, video or audio made or changed by AI.
- Disclosure setting: an option when posting that labels content as AI-made or altered.
Official sources:
- YouTube Help: Disclosing use of altered or synthetic content
Try it now: Look at your last five posts or your next week's plan. For each, decide whether it needs an AI label on your platform and why. Write a short labeling checklist.
You can now label realistic AI content correctly on your platforms.

check.q: Which kind of post is most likely to need an AI label?
options: A realistic AI video of a real place that looks real
A script AI helped you write
A video with auto-captions
A photo with a simple color filter
check.why: Platforms ask you to label realistic AI content that viewers could mistake for real.

check.q: You are not sure whether a post needs an AI label. What would you do?
options: Leave it unlabeled
Delete the post
Label it
Ask followers in the comments
check.why: When unsure, labeling is the safe choice.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Disclosing brand deals the FTC way
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a sponsored post with a clear, correct disclosure.
This lesson builds toward: Given a brand deal or free product, you will write a sponsored post with a clear disclosure at the start, with the disclosure shown and said early and every claim honest.
If a brand pays you, gives you free products, a commission or a trip, and your audience would not expect that connection, you must disclose it, even if you keep a free product and even for small gifts. Disclose on every sponsored post; you cannot assume viewers saw earlier ones.
The FTC's endorsement guidance says disclosures must be easy to notice and understand. "#ad" or "Ad:" at the start, or "Sponsored by XYZ", work well. Vague tags like "#partner", "#ambassador" or "#sp", or disclosures hidden in comments, at the end of long captions, or behind "more", often do not. In videos, disclose in the video itself, ideally both said and shown, and early; repeat it during live streams.
Only say what you honestly believe from real use, and never post fake reviews. Platform disclosure tools help but may not be enough on their own; add your own. AI can draft sponsored captions, but you are responsible for the disclosure and every claim.
Step by step:
- Check if you have a material connection: payment, free product, commission, trip.
- Put "#ad" or "Sponsored" at the start of the caption.
- In videos, say and show it early; repeat during lives.
- Only make claims from your honest experience.
- Use platform tools AND your own disclosure.
Words to know:
- Material connection: a relationship like payment or free products that viewers might not expect.
- Endorsement: a message that viewers think shows your honest opinion of a product.
Official sources:
- FTC: Endorsement Guides, What People Are Asking
Try it now: Write a sample sponsored post with AI help for a product you really use. Put a clear disclosure at the start, write the spoken disclosure for the video, and check every claim is honest.
You can now disclose brand deals clearly and honestly the way the FTC expects.

check.q: Where should a brand-deal disclosure appear in a caption?
options: At the very end, after the hashtags
Only in your profile bio
In a comment under the post
At the start, where people see it first
check.why: A clear disclosure goes where viewers see it right away.

check.q: You are paid to mention a product in a video. What would you do?
options: Mention the deal only in the description
Say and show the disclosure early in the video
Skip the disclosure because the brand is well known
Disclose only if a viewer asks
check.why: In a video the disclosure should be said and shown early.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Protecting your rights and respecting others'
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI without copying others, and protect your own content and likeness.
This lesson builds toward: Using AI tools and brand contracts, you will list rules for using others' work and protecting your own content and likeness, with at least three rules, including no voice or face copying without permission.
Do not use AI to copy another creator's videos, a brand's logo, or someone's voice or face without permission. Making a real person appear to say or do things they did not can mislead viewers, break platform rules and lead to legal claims. Use music and clips you have the rights to, or the platform's licensed library.
Ownership: the US Copyright Office says purely AI-generated material is not protected by copyright, but your own creative work, including your human edits and arrangement, can be. The more your content is your own voice, footage and ideas, the more it is yours.
Protect yourself: read brand contracts for who owns the content, how long they can use it, and whether they can use your face or voice with AI. Keep originals of your work. Have a lawyer review any contract that gives away rights to your content or likeness.
Step by step:
- Never use AI to copy another creator, brand or person's voice or face without permission.
- Use licensed music and clips.
- Put your own voice, footage and ideas at the center.
- Read contracts for ownership, usage time and AI use of your likeness.
- Have a lawyer review contracts that give away rights.
Words to know:
- Likeness: your face, voice and identity.
- License: permission to use something under set terms.
- Usage rights: what a brand may do with your content and for how long.
Official sources:
- US Copyright Office: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
- US Copyright Office: Part 2 Copyrightability report announcement
Try it now: Final task: write three rules you will follow on using others' work and your own rights, then assemble your creator content kit: niche and pillars, 7-day plan, script, repurposed pieces, AI-labeling checklist and sample sponsored post.
You can now create with AI as a creator while keeping your audience's trust and protecting everyone's rights.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Niche, pillars and plan The niche is vague, or the plan has posts that fit no pillar. A clear niche statement, three pillars and a 7-day plan where each post fits a pillar. The plan also mixes formats and says what the audience gets from each post. Script in your voice The script has no hook, sounds unlike you, or has unchecked facts. A short script with a strong hook that sounds like you, with facts checked. You tried more than one hook and can say why you chose this one. Repurposed pieces Fewer than three pieces, or captions with errors. At least three short pieces with correct captions that each make sense alone. Each piece is shaped for the platform it will go on. AI-labeling checklist No checklist, or realistic AI content left unlabeled. A checklist that says when to label AI content on your platforms, including when unsure. It also says where to find each platform's own rule so you can check for changes. Sponsored post disclosure The disclosure is missing, hidden or late. A clear disclosure at the start, plus a spoken disclosure for video, and honest claims. It also plans a repeat disclosure for live streams or long videos. Rights rules Fewer than three rules, or a rule that allows copying others' work or likeness. Three clear rules on using others' work and protecting your own. The rules also cover what to check in a brand contract before signing. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What should you check in a brand contract?
options: Who owns the content, for how long, and AI use of your likeness
Only the payment amount
Only the posting date
The brand's logo colors
check.why: Ownership, time limits and likeness rights protect you and your work.

check.q: A fan asks you to use AI to copy a famous creator's voice for a joke video. What would you do?
options: Do it, since it is only a joke
Do it but add a small note
Do it only on one platform
Say no unless you have that creator's permission
check.why: Copying another person's voice without permission is not okay.
